newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Deutsche Bank trims Luxembourg operations.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Bank trims Luxembourg operations.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG is scaling back operations in Luxembourg, moving part of its euro market loans business to Ireland and proprietary trading to London.
The bank, Germany's largest, said the moves reflected a new group structure, but also growing competitive pressures both in the industry and among financial centres.

"There is a new structure in Deutsche Bank, we are concentrating business in a few places, thus investment banking is now in London," Ekkehard Storck, Deutsche Bank Luxembourg managing director -- a wholly-owned subsidiary of Deutsche Bank -- told a news conference on Wednesday.
His remarks had been embargoed for publication on Friday.

"We are moving proprietary trading to have a better overview and more transparency," he said. The business could go to group headquarters in Frankfurt or to London, with the balance at the moment swinging to London. The move is due by mid-year.
"It is a logical development in the course of globalisation," Storck said.
At the start of the year loan syndication had already been moved from Luxembourg to Frankfurt, where it is now centralised together with acquisition, leaving DB Lux only with sales and distribution.
Storck admitted the move of refinancing activities for euro market credits was "a flight from here. But what can we do when company taxes are only 10 percent in Dublin?"
Deutsche Bank Luxembourg is up shop in Dublin's reduced-tax International Financial Services Centre, where corporate taxes are almost 30 percent below the comparable level in Luxembourg.
Operations at Deutsche Bank/DB Ireland plc with an initial capital of 200 million marks, mainly to refinance euro market credits, are due to start in May.
The capital is to be raised to 500 million marks, enabling the bank to generate lending to the tune of eight billion marks.
Storck said the move became more urgent as margins fell and competitive pressures grew.

Asked what Deutsche would do when a European Union accord which granted the offshore Dublin centre its special status ran out in 2005, Storck said, "Then we will have to think again." London might then become an option.

Storck denied DB Lux was gradually being drained of activities. In the restructuring the subsidiary had been appointed private banking "centre of competence" for Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.
The move to Dublin's IFSC tax haven also reflected expected changes to banks minimum reserve requirements in Europe's 1999 economic and monetary union, which would likely affect refinancing costs.

It also addressed insufficient measures on the part of the Luxembourg government to lower the tax burden on companies, which runs at a total 40 percent in the Grand Duchy. This compares with 10 percent in Dublin.
Finally, labour costs remained relatively high in Luxembourg despite a shift to performance-related pay, Storck said.
In Dublin the bank had had no trouble in finding affordable and qualified staff quickly. Deutsche Bank/DB Ireland plc will employ 18 -- 17 local staff and one German manager.
